props.title: The Fog
props.initialSlug: A deadly mist hides the past.

sections.content: John Carpenter's The Fog (1980) masterfully blends maritime ghost story with small-town horror. Following his breakthrough with Halloween (1978), Carpenter crafted this atmospheric tale of vengeful spirits emerging from a supernatural fog to terrorize a California coastal town. The film established several techniques that would become Carpenter trademarks - wide Panavision shots creating isolation, synthesizer scores building dread, and ensemble casts facing supernatural threats. It shares DNA with other early 80s coastal horror like Dead & Buried (1981) and The Beast Within (1982), but The Fog's ghostly mariners remain uniquely haunting.

sections.content: The film's practical effects and atmospheric cinematography by Dean Cundey create a tangible sense of supernatural menace without relying on gore. The glowing fog itself becomes a character, rolling in with malevolent purpose while concealing its vengeful inhabitants. This approach influenced later atmospheric horror like In the Mouth of Madness (1994) and The Mist (2007). Carpenter regular Adrienne Barbeau leads a strong cast including Jamie Lee Curtis and her mother Janet Leigh, marking their only on-screen collaboration.

The Fog demonstrates Carpenter's mastery of building tension through suggestion rather than explicit violence. The opening campfire story sets up the historical curse while the gradual reveal of the ghostly Blake and his crew maintains mystery. This restraint influenced films like Session 9 (2001) and The Others (2001) which similarly rely on atmosphere over shock value. The film's themes of historical sins returning to haunt the present resonate through later coastal horror like Dead Calm (1989) and Below (2002). SUBHEAD: Maritime Horror Legacy

sections.content: The Fog helped establish maritime horror as a distinct subgenre, influencing films like Deep Rising (1998) and Triangle (2009). The film's blend of historical revenge with supernatural horror created a template followed by Mary (2019) and Haunted Ship (2016). Its emphasis on practical effects over CGI maintains its effectiveness, unlike the effects-heavy 2005 remake which failed to capture the original's atmospheric dread.
